title: Myelin Governs Hippocampal Network Function through the Extracellular Space it Occupies, Not Only the Axons it Insulates
abstract: Myelin, the multilamellar sheath wrapping neuronal axons, enables saltatory conduction. Beyond electrical insulation, myelin occupies volume, and therefore shapes the extracellular space (ECS) through which interstitial fluid flows and neurotransmitter diffuses. How these two roles interact is unknown. We built a multi-scale model of hippocampal CA1 coupling lattice Boltzmann simulations of ECS flow to detailed networks of reconstructed neurons and glia. Demyelination enlarged the ECS volume fraction from 28 to 43 per cent up to 43 to 70 per cent across layers, lowered tortuosity from about 1.7 to 1.4, raised effective diffusivity from 0.35 to 0.50 of free solution and shortened solute breakthrough times by roughly a third, while raising flow speed yet lowering viscous dissipation. Because transmitter concentration scales inversely with that volume, synaptic driving force fell: postsynaptic potential amplitude declined with wrap count and transmission failed entirely below four of sixteen wraps. In 200-cell networks, demyelination halved firing (pyramidal 7.9 to 4.4 Hz), rendered discharge burst-dominated, reduced band power by up to 8.7-fold and displaced the population state, which a classifier separated at 100 per cent accuracy, whereas an inflammatory glial census left every functional measure unchanged. Driving myelin continuously from intact to 12.5 per cent and back recovered the same threshold near four wraps, and firing rate and spectral power returned fully to baseline. Myelin thus governs circuit function through the space it vacates as well as the axons it insulates, with opposite consequences for clearance and for signalling, a dissociation that may matter in demyelinating disease.

reason: Multiscale model reveals how myelin volume and extracellular space critically govern hippocampal network function.
hook: Simulations suggest myelin shapes hippocampal network function by occupying extracellular volume, altering diffusion and flow alongside insulation.

title: Sensory neurons gate a cortical plasticity window for immune encoding
abstract: Activity-dependent plasticity allows brain circuits to encode experience, but this has been established with brief stimuli. Immune responses develop over days and are represented in the insular cortex (IC). How the cortex encodes experiences with this temporal structure is unknown. Here we show that Trpv1+ sensory neurons open a multi-day cortical plasticity window matched to the immune response. Following peripheral immune challenges, Parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory interneurons are activated first, restricting plasticity. Vasoactive intestinal peptide-expressing interneurons respond two days later, disinhibiting IC excitatory neurons. Weaker challenges trigger the first phase but not the second, and preventing the transition blocks immune encoding, whereas lowering inhibition beforehand does not. These results identify a body-to-brain mechanism that gates cortical plasticity on the timescale of slowly evolving physiological experience.

reason: Identifies a sensory-driven cortical plasticity window controlled by distinct interneurons for encoding immune experiences.
hook: Peripheral immune challenges open a multi-day window of cortical plasticity in the insular cortex, regulated by a sequential shift in inhibitory interneuron activity.

title: A multi-institutional investigation of psilocybin's effects on mouse behavior
abstract: Studies reporting the effects of psychedelic drugs on mouse behavior are rapidly emerging. However, the reproducibility and reliability of these effects remain uncertain. Here we implemented a multi-institutional collaborative approach to assess which effects of psilocybin on mouse behavior are robust and replicable. Five independent laboratories performed the same experiments to test the acute and persistent effects of psilocybin (2 mg kg-1, intraperitoneally) on various behaviors. Psilocybin acutely increased anxiety- and avoidance-related behaviors and decreased fear expression in a robust and replicable manner. Surprisingly, however, psilocybin did not have replicable effects 24 h after administration in terms of reducing anxiety- and depression-like behaviors or facilitating fear extinction learning. Additionally, we did not observe psilocybin-induced alterations in social preference or social reward learning. Our characterization of psilocybin's behavioral effects, using ~200 male and female mice per experiment across five laboratories, demonstrates several robust acute effects and suggests that some of psilocybin's reported persistent effects in mice may be modest and/or inconsistent.

reason: Multi-institutional study rigorously challenging reproducible behavioral effects of psychedelics in mice.
hook: Multi-site replication testing shows that while psilocybin acutely alters anxiety and fear responses in mice, previously reported lasting behavioral effects lack consistency across laboratories.

title: Neural dynamics become significantly faster and more nonlinear at the peak of information processing
abstract: The temporal scale at which neural populations preserve stimulus information is often treated as fixed, even though population activity changes rapidly during sensory processing. Whether the information-optimal scale changes within a single stimulus-evoked episode, and what determines its evolution, remains unclear. We developed Integration-Split, a decoding-based framework that estimates the time-varying temporal resolution of population spike trains. Across four visual paradigms and throughout the mouse visual hierarchy, the optimal scale contracted after stimulus onset and subsequently re-expanded. This pattern persisted across stimulus temporal frequencies and was largely absent in a hippocampal control. The optimal scale varied inversely with stimulus decodability, reaching its finest resolution when stimulus identity was most accurately decoded. Beyond this association, independently estimating the signal-noise autocorrelation balance across candidate window widths identified the window that maximized the autocorrelation-based signal-to-noise ratio, and this optimal width closely followed the Integration-Split trajectory. Consistent with these findings, stronger nonlinear predictive structure coincided with finer optimal temporal resolution, consistent with the idea that shorter integration windows are needed to preserve informative nonlinear population structure that would otherwise be attenuated by temporal averaging. To test the functional relevance of this organization, we trained a Transformer solely to decode stimulus identity, without providing the optimal temporal-scale pattern or Integration-Split outputs. Its learned attention exhibited a similar contraction-and-recovery profile, and disrupting heads with stronger correspondence produced larger decoding deficits. Together, these findings reveal a dynamically changing, information-optimal temporal scale in population coding, shaped by the evolving balance of signal and noise autocorrelation and by nonlinear population structure, and independently recapitulated in the learned attention of a Transformer trained without temporal-scale supervision.

reason: Neural dynamics speed up and become nonlinear at peak sensory information processing.
hook: Neural population timescales contract to finer resolutions during peak sensory processing, matching shifts in signal-to-noise balance and nonlinear dynamics.

title: Mapping AMPA and NMDA receptors at mouse brain hippocampal synapses by cryo-ET
abstract: AMPA and NMDA receptors are fundamental to synaptic transmission through the detection of released neurotransmitter. These ion channels open in response to glutamate binding, resulting in depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane and influx of calcium. Receptor localization plays a key role in synaptic strength, and changes in receptor number and location underpin synaptic plasticity, learning and memory. Here we apply receptor subunit-specific antibody fragments and multiplexed gold nanoparticle conjugates, together with cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), to elucidate the in-situ molecular organization of AMPA and NMDA receptors at hippocampal synapses in adult mouse brain tissue. AMPA receptors are predominantly found in densely packed liquid-like clusters, with interspersed NMDA receptors and adjacent NMDA receptor clusters. By direct localization of individual receptors, we provide molecular-resolution insight into the distribution of AMPA and NMDA receptors across the synapse, at peri and extrasynaptic sites, and within endocytosed vesicles. Visualization of multiple presynaptic vesicle fusion events suggests that receptors are near, but not always directly adjacent to, transmitter release sites. By mapping AMPA and NMDA receptors, and glutamate release sites, we provide receptor-resolution insight into the structure and function of brain hippocampal synapses.

These ion channels open in response to glutamate binding, resulting in depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane and influx of calcium. Receptor localization plays a key role in…
reason: Maps in situ molecular organization of AMPA and NMDA receptors at hippocampal synapses using cryo-ET.
hook: AMPA receptors form densely packed clusters with interspersed NMDA receptors at mouse hippocampal synapses, according to a cryo-electron tomography preprint.

title: Hypothalamus-driven brain health through metabolic flexibility
abstract: Organismal physiology depends on continuous, non-hierarchical communication among cells, tissues, and organs. We argue that this communication rests on metabolic flexibility-the capacity of cells and tissues to adapt substrate use to changing energetic demands-and that the hypothalamus serves as the central hub coordinating this flexibility across the body. Using hypothalamic agouti-related protein (AgRP) and pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons as a model, we show these melanocortin neurons do more than regulate hunger and satiety: by integrating metabolic, hormonal, and immune signals, they shape reward, learning, executive function, and social behavior, while imposing coordinated metabolic states on peripheral tissues. When this flexibility is lost, as with aging or overnutrition, body-brain communication becomes rigid, driving cognitive decline, chronic inflammation, and neurodegenerative disease. We propose that signals from the body are not peripheral modifiers of brain function but fundamental determinants of it, with direct implications for hypothalamus-centered strategies to preserve brain health across the lifespan.

reason: Proposes the hypothalamus coordinates whole-body metabolic flexibility to preserve brain health.
hook: Hypothalamic melanocortin neurons coordinate whole-body metabolism and shape cognition. Losing this metabolic flexibility impairs body-brain communication, potentially driving neurodegeneration.
